examples: The judge admonished the jury to disregard the remark.
Her editor admonished her for missing a second deadline.
We were admonished against discussing the case outside the room.
He admonished the team that another lapse would mean suspension.
The coach admonished the players to stop arguing with the referee.
She admonished me gently, and I took the point.
entries.русский: увещевать, делать замечание — предостережение с упрёком, книжн.
entries.patterns: admonish + sb + to-infinitive · admonish + sb + that-clause · admonish + sb + for + -ing · admonish + sb + against + -ing · admonish + sb (bare object: she admonished me gently)
entries.never: admonish to do something without an object, and admonish someone from doing. The preposition is against for the warning sense and for for the rebuking sense: admonished her for interrupting, admonished her against interrupting again. There is no mandative clause — ✗ admonished that he be present — and no gerund complement: ✗ admonished interrupting.
entries.reports: a warning delivered from a position of authority, mixed with mild reproach — unlike caution, which implies no fault on the hearer's part, admonish says the hearer has already gone wrong or is about to.
entries.see also: caution, warn, counsel, urge, command, charge

examples: Her lawyer advised her to say nothing until the hearing.
I'd advise waiting until the prices come down.
The doctor advised that he stay off the ankle for two weeks.
We advise against booking through a third party.
The manual advises what to do if the light stays red.
Please advise us of any change in your billing address.
She advised me that the deadline had already passed.
Her agent advised her what to say if anyone asked about the delay.
entries.pronunciation note: the noun advice is /ədˈvaɪs/, ad-VYSE, with an /s/ and no plural
entries.русский: советовать — общий глагол совета; в обороте advise sb of sth — офиц. «извещать»
entries.patterns: advise + sb + to-infinitive · advise + that-clause (subjunctive) · advise + sb + that-clause · advise + -ing · advise + sb + against + -ing · advise + (sb) + wh-clause · advise + noun phrase · advise + sb + of + noun phrase
entries.never: advise to do something with no object — this is the quiet error inside an otherwise well-behaved verb: ✗ I advise to book early → ✓ I advise booking early / I advise you to book early. The infinitive needs somebody to attach to. Also advise someone from doing something — the preposition is against: advised us against selling. And do not write the noun: I adviced him is not a word.
entries.spelling: advise is spelled -ise in American English too. It is not one of the -ize/-ise pairs, because the ending is not the Greek suffix; advize is wrong everywhere. The noun advice is uncountable — ✗ an advice, ✗ some advices → ✓ a piece of advice, some advice.
entries.subjunctive: advise takes the bare mandative form — advised that she be notified, not that she is notified. Of the four subjunctive verbs in this file it is the one most tolerant of should, but the bare form is still standard American.
entries.reports: the general-purpose advice verb, and the only common one that works in all three frames — object plus infinitive, gerund, and subjunctive clause. Weaker than urge, more authoritative than suggest. The advise someone of something pattern is a separate, bureaucratic sense meaning formally inform: Please advise us of any change of address.
entries.see also: counsel, recommend, suggest, urge, caution, inform

examples: The report advocates a phased rollout rather than a single launch.
He has advocated for years that the deposit be refundable.
Nobody at the meeting advocated cutting the program entirely.
She advocates for families going through the appeals process.
The senator advocated an immediate freeze on new permits.
They advocate replacing the whole system, which strikes me as expensive.
Two members advocated against holding the vote before the audit.
entries.pronunciation note: the noun is /ˈædvəkət/, AD-vuh-kut, with a reduced last syllable — the two are spelled alike and said differently
entries.русский: выступать за, отстаивать — публично поддерживать курс или меру, книжн.
entries.patterns: advocate + noun phrase · advocate + -ing · advocate + that-clause (subjunctive) · advocate for + noun phrase or -ing · advocate against + noun phrase or -ing
entries.never: advocate someone to do something, and advocate to do something — the verb takes no infinitive at all, with or without an object: ✗ advocates to build more housing. Repairs: advocated that they be released, advocated releasing them, advocated their release.
entries.reports: open, public support for a policy or course of action — a recommendation made to an audience rather than to an individual. Unlike suggest, it implies the speaker has taken a side and will defend it.
entries.contested: advocate for was condemned for a century as a redundancy, on the grounds that advocate is already transitive. That battle is over in American English: advocate for a cause, advocate for patients is now standard, and it is the only natural option when the object is a person or group rather than a proposal. Keep the bare transitive for policies (advocates a flat tax) and use for for constituencies (advocates for veterans).
entries.see also: endorse, propose, recommend, push, argue

examples: A neighbor alerted the fire department.
She alerted me to a typo on the first page.
The bank alerted him that his card had been used overseas.
Nobody alerted the night shift to the change in procedure.
The app alerts you when your balance drops below fifty dollars.
We should alert legal before this goes any further.
entries.русский: предупредить, известить — обратить чьё-то внимание на факт или риск, без указаний
entries.patterns: alert + sb + to + noun phrase · alert + sb + to the fact + that-clause · alert + sb + that-clause · alert + noun phrase
entries.never: alert someone to do something — there is no infinitive frame, and the trap is that to is already the verb's preposition, so the wrong sentence looks right. ✗ alerted us to check the logs → ✓ alerted us that the logs needed checking, or simply told us to check the logs. And no bare alert that: an object is required, ✗ alerted that the servers were down. There is no subjunctive either: the that-clause states a fact.
entries.reports: giving someone notice of something they need to know about now, usually a risk or an anomaly. Neutral about blame and silent about what to do next, which is what separates it from warn — you alert someone to a fact, you warn them about a consequence.
entries.see also: tip off, warn, forewarn, flag, notify

examples: The mayor cautioned residents to stay off the roads until morning.
Economists cautioned that the drop might be seasonal.
He cautioned me against making an offer on the first day.
The label cautions users about mixing the two solutions.
She cautioned that the numbers had not been audited.
I'd caution you to get that in writing.
entries.русский: предостерегать — сдержанное «будьте осторожны», книжн., частое в прессе
entries.patterns: caution + sb + to-infinitive · caution + sb + against + -ing · caution + sb + that-clause · caution + that-clause · caution + sb + about + noun phrase or -ing
entries.never: caution someone from doing something — it is against, like warn and advise: cautioned investors against reading too much into one quarter. And caution that + subjunctive: despite the family resemblance to advise and urge, caution is not a mandative trigger, and its that-clause is an ordinary indicative statement. ✗ cautioned that the fee be waived → ✓ cautioned against waiving the fee / cautioned them not to waive the fee.
entries.british: in British usage caution has a police sense with no American equivalent — to caution a suspect is to read them the formal warning before questioning, and a caution is a recorded reprimand issued instead of a prosecution. He was cautioned therefore means something much more specific in Britain than in the United States.
entries.reports: a measured, unalarmed warning — the register of press releases and analysts. Warn says danger; caution says be careful. Note that the objectless caution that is common in reporting (Officials cautioned that the figures were preliminary), where the equivalent warn that would sound more dire.
entries.see also: warn, admonish, advise, alert

examples: It took an hour, but she convinced the committee to reconsider.
Nothing I said convinced him that the check had cleared.
The evidence convinced the jury of his innocence.
I'm not convinced the second option is any cheaper.
He convinced his parents to let him take a year off.
She convinced herself that nobody had noticed.
entries.русский: убедить (в чём-то) — добиться, чтобы человек поверил; глагол результата
entries.patterns: convince + sb + that-clause · convince + sb + of + noun phrase · convince + sb + to-infinitive
entries.never: convince that with no object — someone has to be convinced: ✗ He convinced that the plan would work → ✓ He convinced us that it would work. And convince someone into doing something is not idiomatic; that frame belongs to talk into and persuade.
entries.reports: a change of belief that actually took hold. The verb is a success verb — you cannot convince someone who remains unconvinced — which distinguishes it from urge and press, both of which report only the attempt.
entries.contested: the traditional rule says convince takes belief (convince that, convince of) and persuade takes action (persuade to do), so convince her to resign was long treated as an error. In current American English it is entirely standard, appears throughout edited prose, and no ordinary reader notices. Use it. The distinction still does real work in the other direction: I convinced him that he was wrong and I persuaded him to admit it are not the same claim.
entries.see also: persuade, talk into, win over, prevail on

examples: His advisor counseled him to defer the semester rather than withdraw.
The elders counseled patience.
We were counseled against putting anything in writing.
She counsels students on financial aid appeals.
The report counsels that the review be conducted by an outside firm.
He counseled restraint, and for once everyone listened.
entries.pronunciation note: identical in sound to council, which is a body of people and never a verb
entries.русский: советовать, рекомендовать — совет профессионала или совет особой важности, книжн.
entries.patterns: counsel + sb + to-infinitive · counsel + sb + against + -ing · counsel + that-clause (subjunctive) · counsel + noun phrase · counsel + sb + on/about + noun phrase
entries.never: counsel someone from doing something, and counseled that he should be removed is British-flavored — American practice takes the bare subjunctive, counseled that he be removed. The bare gerund is not the frame either: prefer a noun, counsel delay, over ✗ counsel delaying.
entries.british: the past and the -ing form double the l in British spelling — counselled, counselling, counsellor — against American counseled, counseling, counselor. Every example below uses the American form.
entries.reports: advice given in a professional or pastoral capacity, or advice with unusual gravity. Counsel patience, counsel restraint, counsel delay — the bare noun-phrase frame — are the set collocations of this verb, the formal counterpart of advise caution. Reach for the noun rather than a gerund: ✓ counseled delay, ✗ counseled delaying.
entries.see also: advise, admonish, recommend, urge

examples: The fine is too small to deter anyone.
Bad reviews deterred her from booking the same hotel again.
Nothing we said deterred him from going.
Higher premiums have deterred younger drivers from buying coverage.
The lock is mostly there to deter casual thieves.
She was not deterred by the first rejection.
The new fee has deterred a number of families from the program.
entries.pronunciation note: the past is deterred, with a doubled r
entries.русский: удерживать, отпугивать — не дать сделать; чаще о причине-обстоятельстве, а не о словах
entries.patterns: deter + sb + from + -ing · deter + sb + from + noun phrase · deter + noun phrase (a person or an activity: deter casual thieves, deter theft)
entries.never: deter someone to do something, deter someone doing something, and deter someone against doing something. The only preposition is from. There is no that-clause: ✗ deterred him that it was risky.
entries.reports: the effect rather than the words — that something stopped a person from acting, whether or not anyone spoke. Its subject is more often a circumstance than a person (the price deterred us), which is what separates it from dissuade, where somebody argued you out of it.
entries.see also: dissuade, discourage, talk out of, warn, prohibit

examples: The building discourages deliveries after nine.
My advisor discouraged me from taking two labs in the same term.
Rain discouraged most of the crowd.
The policy is meant to discourage speculative bidding.
Nothing anybody said discouraged her from trying again.
We discourage photography in the reading room.
The forecast discouraged half the group from the longer route.
entries.русский: отговаривать, не поощрять — мягко противодействовать действию; антоним encourage
entries.patterns: discourage + sb + from + -ing · discourage + sb + from + noun phrase · discourage + -ing · discourage + noun phrase
entries.never: discourage someone to do something and discourage someone against doing something. No that-clause either: ✗ discouraged us that we should apply. And note the asymmetry with its opposite: encourage takes an object plus an infinitive, discourage never does — ✓ encouraged me to apply but ✗ discouraged me to apply → ✓ discouraged me from applying.
entries.reports: the exact opposite number of encourage, and the mildest of the from + -ing group — it reports advice or a policy that pushes against an action without forbidding it. The bare gerund frame is the natural way to state a blanket policy: The city discourages idling.
entries.see also: dissuade, deter, encourage, talk out of, ban

examples: His friends dissuaded him from posting the whole thread.
I tried to dissuade her from driving through the pass at night.
Nothing could dissuade them from selling the house.
She was easily dissuaded.
The realtor dissuaded us from bidding above asking.
He talked for an hour and dissuaded nobody.
Her family dissuaded her from the whole scheme in a single evening.
entries.русский: отговорить — успешно убедить не делать; книжн., разг. соответствие — talk out of
entries.type: reporting verb — persuasion away from an action
entries.patterns: dissuade + sb + from + -ing · dissuade + sb + from + noun phrase · dissuade + sb (+ from it)
entries.never: dissuade someone to do something, dissuade someone of doing something, dissuade someone against doing. Only from. There is no positive verb ✗ suade — the opposite of dissuade is persuade.
entries.reports: successful argument against a course of action — the person had intended to do it and, after the conversation, did not. That success condition is what separates it from discourage, which reports only the push. The near-synonym in ordinary speech is talk out of; dissuade is what you write, talked her out of it is what you say.
entries.see also: talk out of, deter, discourage, persuade

examples: The crowd egged him on until he climbed the fence.
Don't egg her on; she'll actually do it.
They egged each other on all afternoon.
He needed no egging on.
Two of them egged the argument on from the sidelines.
She egged me on to send the email, and I have regretted it since.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on on; unrelated to the noun egg, from an Old Norse word eggja meaning to goad — the same root as edge
entries.русский: подбивать, подначивать — разг.: подстрекать на что-то безрассудное
entries.type: reporting verb — encouragement toward something unwise
entries.patterns: egg + sb + on · egg + sb + on + to-infinitive (less common)
entries.never: egg on him — with a pronoun object the particle must follow it: egged him on, egged them on, never ✗ egged on him. (With a full noun phrase both orders occur — egged the crowd on and egged on the crowd — but the split order is the usual one, and the passive egged on by his friends is the commonest form of all.) There is no that-clause and no gerund frame: ✗ egged him on doing it.
entries.reports: urging someone toward behavior the reporter considers reckless or ill-advised. The judgment is built in: nobody is ever egged on to do something sensible.
entries.see also: encourage, talk into, nudge, push

examples: His teacher encouraged him to submit the story to a magazine.
The program encourages composting.
She encouraged us to ask questions at any point.
Low rates have encouraged borrowing.
Nobody encouraged her; she just did it.
I was encouraged to hear the schedule had not slipped.
entries.русский: поощрять, подбадривать — побуждать к тому, что говорящий считает полезным
entries.patterns: encourage + sb + to-infinitive · encourage + -ing · encourage + noun phrase · encourage + sb + in + noun phrase
entries.never: encourage that with a subjunctive clause — ✗ encouraged that he apply → ✓ encouraged him to apply. And encourage someone that: it takes no that-clause of any kind. The infinitive also needs an object — ✗ The policy encourages to recycle → ✓ encourages recycling / encourages residents to recycle.
entries.reports: positive pressure toward an action the speaker considers good for the hearer. Softer than urge, warmer than advise, and unlike either it says nothing about the speaker's expertise — you encourage a friend, you advise a client.
entries.see also: urge, nudge, push, egg on, discourage

examples: Two former governors endorsed the measure.
The union declined to endorse either candidate.
She endorsed the report without reservation.
The committee endorsed a phased rollout.
He endorsed her for the vacancy.
Nobody outside the department endorsed the plan.
entries.русский: публично одобрить, поддержать — поставить своё имя за предложение, кандидата или товар
entries.patterns: endorse + noun phrase · endorse + sb + for + noun phrase · endorse the idea/view + of + -ing
entries.never: endorse someone to do something, endorse to do something, and endorse that the plan go forward. Endorse takes a noun phrase and nothing else: ✓ endorsed the proposal, ✗ endorsed postponing the vote is at best marginal — write endorsed a postponement. It takes no that-clause of any kind, indicative or subjunctive; to attach a clause you need a noun for it to hang on, endorsed the view that the vote should wait.
entries.reports: putting one's name behind a proposal, candidate, or product. Weaker as a speech act than advocate — endorsing is a single public act of approval, advocating is a sustained campaign.
entries.see also: advocate, recommend, propose, put forward, second

examples: The letter enjoins members to attend in person.
A federal judge enjoined the state from enforcing the rule.
She enjoined us to silence about what we had seen.
The order enjoined that the records be preserved.
Scripture enjoins charity toward strangers.
The court enjoined further construction pending review.
entries.русский: предписывать, наказывать (что-л. сделать); юр. запрещать судебным приказом — книжн.
entries.type: reporting verb — solemn urging, or legal prohibition
entries.patterns: enjoin + sb + to-infinitive · enjoin + that-clause (subjunctive) · enjoin + sb + from + -ing · enjoin + sb + to + noun phrase (enjoined us to silence) · enjoin + noun phrase (enjoin silence)
entries.never: enjoin someone against doing something — the legal preposition is from.
entries.two opposite senses: this verb means both urge strongly and forbid by court order, and the frame tells you which. With to-infinitive it urges: enjoined us to be patient. With from + -ing it prohibits: enjoined the company from selling the data. Nothing else disambiguates them, so keep the frames clean.
entries.reports: in the urging sense, a solemn charge laid on someone; in the legal sense, an injunction. Both are markedly formal — in ordinary speech use urge or ban.
entries.see also: exhort, urge, admonish, counsel, forbid, prohibit

examples: The captain exhorted the crew to keep bailing.
She exhorted her students to read outside the syllabus.
The editorial exhorts voters to turn out in November.
He exhorted the congregation to generosity.
Coaches exhorted the players to one more effort.
The pamphlet exhorts readers to write their representatives.
entries.pronunciation note: the h is silent and the x is voiced, /ɡz/ — not eks-HORT
entries.русский: призывать, увещевать — горячий публичный призыв, книжн., ритор.
entries.patterns: exhort + sb + to-infinitive · exhort + sb + to + noun phrase · exhort + that-clause (subjunctive — archaic, biblical: I exhort that supplications be made)
entries.never: exhort to do something without an object, and exhort someone doing something. The frame is fixed: a person, then an infinitive.
entries.reports: urging with emotional heat and usually in public — a speech to a crowd rather than a word to a friend. Stronger and more sermon-like than urge; nobody exhorts you to try the fish.
entries.see also: urge, enjoin, press, admonish, implore, beseech

examples: He flagged two errors in the appendix.
I flagged the invoice for review.
She flagged that the numbers hadn't been reconciled yet.
The system flags any transaction over ten thousand dollars.
Legal flagged the indemnity clause as a problem.
Nobody flagged what the delay would do to the launch date.
entries.pronunciation note: the past is flagged, with a doubled g
entries.русский: отметить, обратить внимание на — разг.-деловое: указать на возможную проблему
entries.register: informal to neutral; standard workplace English
entries.type: reporting verb — raising something for attention
entries.patterns: flag + noun phrase · flag + that-clause · flag + noun phrase + for/to + sb · flag + wh-clause · flag + noun phrase + as + noun phrase
entries.never: flag someone to do something and flag someone that — the person takes a preposition, not a direct-object slot: ✗ flagged me that the date moved → ✓ flagged to me that the date moved, or better, told me the date had moved.
entries.reports: calling attention to a problem, usually early and usually without claiming it is serious. The office cousin of alert: you flag a risk to a colleague, you alert a colleague to a danger. It is fully standard in workplace writing and still too casual for formal prose, where note or point out is the safer choice.
entries.see also: alert, tip off, caution, warn, point out, note

examples: She floated the idea of a four-day week.
Somebody floated a merger, and the room went quiet.
He floated the plan past his manager before writing it up.
The mayor has floated several sites for the new depot.
They floated the possibility of doing it remotely.
I floated it in the meeting and got nowhere.
He floated moving the deadline, and nobody objected.
entries.русский: закинуть идею, вбросить предложение — высказать пробно, чтобы увидеть реакцию
entries.patterns: float + noun phrase (float an idea) · float the idea/possibility of + -ing · float + noun phrase + to/past + sb · float + that-clause (informal, journalistic) · float + -ing (rare: floated postponing the vote)
entries.never: float someone to do something and float to do something. Like the rest of Group B it takes no personal object; the person you floated it to follows to or past. The that-clause is indicative — ✗ floated that we postpone → ✓ floated the idea of postponing / floated that we might postpone.
entries.reports: putting a suggestion out deliberately unfinished, to see how people react before committing to it. Weaker than propose and weaker even than suggest — floating an idea is explicitly reversible, which is the whole point of choosing the word.
entries.see also: suggest, propose, put forward, advocate, mention

examples: We had been forewarned about the noise from the construction site.
Nobody forewarned him that the interview would run three hours.
She forewarned us of the cost before we signed anything.
Forewarned is forearmed.
The letter forewarned residents of the road closure.
I wish somebody had forewarned me.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on the second syllable, unlike the noun forewarning
entries.русский: заранее предупредить — книжн., подчёркивает, что было время подготовиться
entries.patterns: forewarn + sb + that-clause · forewarn + sb + of/about + noun phrase · forewarn + sb + to-infinitive (uncommon)
entries.never: forewarn that with no object, and forewarn someone from doing. An object is obligatory in the active.
entries.reports: the same act as warn with the timing made explicit — the warning came before the event, and the hearer therefore had a chance to prepare. It appears most often in the passive (I had been forewarned) and in the proverb forewarned is forearmed. In the active it can sound faintly literary; plain warn usually does the job.
entries.see also: warn, alert, caution, tip off, notify

examples: They invited us to stay for dinner.
The chair invited comment from the floor.
She invited him over for coffee after the meeting.
Candidates are invited to submit a portfolio.
He invited me along without asking the others.
The design invites comparison with the older model.
entries.pronunciation note: the noun invite (a dinner invite) is /ˈɪnvaɪt/, IN-vyte, and is informal
entries.русский: приглашать, предлагать — просьба в форме приглашения; часто вежливое требование
entries.patterns: invite + sb + to-infinitive · invite + sb + to + noun phrase · invite + sb + for + noun phrase · invite + noun phrase (invite comment) · invite + sb + over/in/along
entries.never: invite someone that and invite that, and invite someone come — the second verb always takes to. An object is required in the active: ✗ He invited to sit down.
entries.reports: a request framed as an offer — the hearer gains something by complying, which is what separates it from every other verb in this file. Note that invite someone to do is often a polite institutional command in disguise: Applicants are invited to submit a writing sample is not optional.
entries.see also: encourage, urge, suggest, press, ask, request

examples: He moved that the meeting be adjourned.
The defense moved to dismiss the case.
She moved an amendment striking the second clause.
A member moved that the vote be taken by ballot.
Counsel moved for a continuance.
Nobody moved that the item be reconsidered.
entries.русский: вносить предложение (на собрании) — парламентское: предлагать поставить на голосование
entries.type: reporting verb — formal proposal to a meeting
entries.patterns: move + that-clause (subjunctive) · move + to-infinitive (move to adjourn) · move + noun phrase (move an amendment) · move for + noun phrase
entries.never: move someone to do something in this sense — move with an object plus infinitive belongs to the emotional sense (the story moved her to tears) and cannot report a proposal. And move that the meeting is adjourned: the clause verb must be the bare base form.
entries.subjunctive: move is the most reliable subjunctive trigger in the language, because the formula is fixed: I move that the minutes be approved, moved that the item be tabled, moved that the committee not meet in August. The indicative here is simply an error.
entries.reports: a proposal formally put before a deliberative body for a vote — a technical use of propose with a procedural consequence. Outside meetings and courtrooms it is out of place: you do not move that your family get takeout.
entries.see also: propose, put forward, recommend, advocate, stipulate

examples: His sister nudged him to call their mother.
The default setting nudges users toward the annual plan.
I nudged her about the reimbursement form again.
A well-placed question nudged the conversation back on topic.
They nudged us into signing before the deadline.
Nobody nudged him; he volunteered.
entries.русский: подталкивать, мягко напоминать — разг.: ненавязчиво побуждать; также «напомнить»
entries.patterns: nudge + sb + to-infinitive · nudge + sb + toward/into + noun phrase or -ing · nudge + sb + about + noun phrase (the reminder sense) · nudge + sb (bare object)
entries.never: nudge someone that and nudge that. No clause of any kind follows it.
entries.reports: low-pressure encouragement, repeated if necessary — the word chosen precisely to disclaim force. It has a second workplace sense, closer to remind: I nudged him about the invoice means a follow-up message, not persuasion.
entries.see also: encourage, prompt, press, steer, remind

examples: She persuaded the landlord to waive the fee.
It took three phone calls to persuade him.
He persuaded us that the detour would be faster, and he was wrong.
They persuaded her into buying the extended warranty.
I couldn't persuade anyone to come with me.
The evidence persuaded the judge of his good faith.
entries.русский: убедить, уговорить (сделать) — глагол результата: человек согласился и сделал
entries.patterns: persuade + sb + to-infinitive · persuade + sb + that-clause · persuade + sb + of + noun phrase · persuade + sb + into + -ing · persuade + sb + out of + -ing
entries.never: persuade to do something with no object and persuade that with no object — the person persuaded is obligatory: ✗ She persuaded that we should wait → ✓ She persuaded us to wait. And persuade someone doing something.
entries.reports: successful urging that produced an action. This is a success verb: if the person did not budge, you did not persuade them, you urged or pressed them. The success/attempt line runs through the whole file, and it is worth having in one table:
entries.see also: convince, talk into, prevail on, win over, dissuade

examples: Her doctor prescribed a lower dose.
The statute prescribes a thirty-day notice period.
He prescribed rest and a great deal of water.
Nothing in the bylaws prescribes how the chair is chosen.
The regulation prescribes that each unit be inspected annually.
She was prescribed physical therapy instead of surgery.
entries.русский: предписывать, назначать — рекомендация с властью врача или закона, книжн.
entries.patterns: prescribe + noun phrase · prescribe + noun phrase + for + sb · prescribe + that-clause (subjunctive)
entries.never: prescribe someone to do something — like the rest of Group B it takes no object plus infinitive: ✗ prescribed me to rest → ✓ prescribed rest, prescribed that I rest for a week. And prescribe someone something as a double object is shaky in careful writing; prefer prescribed an antibiotic for her.
entries.confusable: prescribe and proscribe are opposites. Prescribe means order or recommend; proscribe means forbid. A regimen the doctor prescribed and a practice the code proscribes say contradictory things about the same activity.
entries.reports: a recommendation that carries institutional authority — a doctor's order, a statute's requirement. Where recommend leaves the choice open, prescribe does not.
entries.see also: recommend, advise, counsel, propose, require, mandate, proscribe

examples: Reporters pressed the governor for a timeline.
He pressed her to reconsider, and she refused.
They pressed him on what he had known and when.
The union is pressing for a shorter workweek.
She didn't press the point.
I was pressed to explain where the money had gone.
He was pressed into chairing the session when the moderator canceled.
entries.русский: настойчиво уговаривать, наседать — давить, ничего не говоря об успехе
entries.patterns: press + sb + to-infinitive · press + sb + for + noun phrase · press + sb + on/about + noun phrase · press for + noun phrase · press + sb + into + -ing (usually passive: was pressed into helping) · press + noun phrase (press the point)
entries.never: press someone that — no that-clause follows it, and no subjunctive. And press someone into to do something: after into comes a gerund or a noun, never an infinitive. The set phrase is press someone into service; with a verb it is pressed into serving.
entries.reports: urging kept up past the point of comfort. It reports repetition and pressure, not success — you can press someone all week and get nowhere, which is exactly what separates it from persuade.
entries.see also: urge, push, persuade, exhort, nag

examples: We finally prevailed on him to take a few days off.
She was prevailed upon to say a few words.
They prevailed on the landlord to extend the lease by a month.
I could not prevail on anyone to trade shifts.
His colleagues prevailed upon him to withdraw the letter.
The board prevailed on the founder to stay through the transition.
entries.pronunciation note: also prevail upon, /prɪˈveɪl əˌpɑn/, which is even more formal
entries.русский: уговорить, склонить — книжн.: добиться согласия у неохотного человека
entries.patterns: prevail on/upon + sb + to-infinitive
entries.never: prevail someone to do something — the preposition is obligatory. And prevail on someone that, prevail on someone into doing. This verb has exactly one frame.
entries.reports: persuading a reluctant person to do something, usually as a favor and usually after some effort. It is a success verb like persuade, but it carries the extra information that the person had to be brought around. Distinctly formal — in speech, talked her into it.
entries.see also: persuade, talk into, win over, press

examples: The audit prompted a full review of the vendor list.
She prompted him with the first two words and he took it from there.
What prompted you to call?
The system prompts you for a second password.
Complaints prompted the store to change its return policy.
A single question prompted an hour of explanation.
entries.русский: побудить, подтолкнуть; подсказать — чаще о событии-причине или о реплике-подсказке
entries.type: reporting verb — causing someone to act or speak
entries.patterns: prompt + sb + to-infinitive · prompt + noun phrase · prompt + sb + for + noun phrase · prompt + sb + with + noun phrase
entries.never: prompt someone that and prompt that. No clause follows it.
entries.reports: supplying the trigger for an action, often without any advice being given at all — the subject is more often an event than a person (the outage prompted a review). When the subject is a person, it means a small verbal push or a supplied cue, as with an actor who has forgotten a line.
entries.see also: nudge, encourage, press, push, remind

examples: The committee proposed a two-year pilot.
He proposed meeting halfway, in Denver.
She proposed that the fee be waived for first-time applicants.
What do you propose we do about it?
The city proposes to widen the intersection next spring.
Nobody proposed an alternative.
The department proposed her as interim chair.
entries.русский: предлагать — формальное предложение, которое можно принять к исполнению
entries.patterns: propose + that-clause (subjunctive) · propose + -ing · propose + to-infinitive (= intend) · propose + noun phrase · propose + noun phrase + to + sb · propose + sb + for/as + noun phrase (nominate: proposed her for the chair)
entries.never: propose someone to do something and propose to someone to do something. Repairs: proposed that we meet, proposed meeting, proposed a meeting. The one place a person may follow propose directly is the nominating sense, where the person is the thing proposed, not the person spoken to: ✓ proposed him as treasurer, still ✗ proposed him to serve as treasurer.
entries.subjunctive: bare base form — proposed that the deadline be extended, proposed that the rule not apply to renewals. The should version is British; the indicative, ✗ proposed that the deadline is extended, is an error in both dialects.
entries.two frames, two meanings: propose to do means the subject intends to do it; propose doing means the subject suggests it be done. He proposed to sell the building is his own plan; He proposed selling the building is a recommendation to the group. A third sense, propose to someone, is an offer of marriage and takes no complement at all.
entries.reports: a suggestion put forward formally enough to be acted on — more procedural than suggest, less binding than move.
entries.see also: suggest, recommend, move, put forward, float

examples: His parents pushed him to apply to law school.
Advocates are pushing for stricter labeling rules.
Don't let anyone push you into signing today.
She pushed the proposal through in two meetings.
The board pushed management to cut costs before the quarter closed.
I'm not going to push it.
entries.pronunciation note: the vowel is /ʊ/ as in put, not /ʌ/ as in hush
entries.русский: давить, настойчиво склонять — с намёком, что человек не хочет; push for — добиваться
entries.patterns: push + sb + to-infinitive · push for + noun phrase · push + sb + into + -ing · push + noun phrase (push a proposal)
entries.never: push someone that. No that-clause. And push someone to doing something — after the object it is a plain infinitive, or into plus a gerund.
entries.reports: sustained pressure toward an action, with a hint that the person being pushed would rather not. Push for reports campaigning for an outcome rather than pressuring a person, and is the neutral option in news writing.
entries.see also: press, urge, nudge, advocate, demand

examples: He put forward three names for the vacancy.
The paper puts forward a theory nobody had considered.
She put the amendment forward on the last day of the session.
The idea was put forward years ago and quietly dropped.
They put him forward as a compromise candidate.
Nobody put forward a serious objection.
entries.русский: выдвигать, предлагать — вынести имя, версию или план на рассмотрение
entries.type: reporting verb — offering a proposal or view
entries.patterns: put forward + noun phrase · put + noun phrase + forward · put forward the idea/view/argument + that-clause · put + sb + forward (as a candidate)
entries.never: put forward someone to do something and put forward to do something. The clause frame requires a noun to hang on: ✗ put forward that we postpone → ✓ put forward the idea that we postpone, or just proposed postponing.
entries.separable: with a pronoun object the particle must follow it — put it forward, never put forward it. With a full noun phrase either order works: put forward a proposal / put a proposal forward.
entries.reports: offering something for consideration — a name, a theory, a plan. More tentative than propose and much more tentative than move; it says the idea is now on the table, not that the speaker is fighting for it.
entries.see also: propose, float, suggest, move, advocate, submit, posit

examples: She recommended a mechanic on Third Street.
The panel recommended that the policy be rewritten from scratch.
I'd recommend getting there half an hour early.
He recommended the book to everyone he met that summer.
The report recommends against expanding the program.
Can you recommend somewhere quiet to work?
Her advisor recommended what to take in the spring.
Two of her professors recommended her for the fellowship.
entries.русский: рекомендовать — совет со знанием дела; решение остаётся за слушающим
entries.patterns: recommend + that-clause (subjunctive) · recommend + -ing · recommend + noun phrase · recommend + noun phrase + to + sb · recommend + sb + for/as + noun phrase · recommend against + -ing · recommend + wh-clause
entries.never: recommend someone to do something and recommend someone something. Both are extremely common learner errors and both have easy repairs: ✗ recommended me to apply → ✓ recommended that I apply / recommended applying; ✗ recommended me a hotel → ✓ recommended a hotel to me. A person may follow recommend only when the person is what is being recommended — ✓ recommended her for the job, ✓ recommended him as a tutor — never when the person is the one being advised.
entries.subjunctive: bare base form — recommended that he see a specialist, recommended that the fee be waived, recommended that she not travel. British writing often prefers recommended that he should see a specialist; American writing takes the bare form, and ✗ recommended that he sees is wrong in both.
entries.contested: recommend someone to do is not quite dead in British English, where it turns up in older writing and still passes with some readers. In American English it is simply wrong, and it is the second most common version of the suggest error. Avoid it in both dialects.
entries.reports: advice offered as the speaker's considered opinion, usually with some claim to knowledge behind it — stronger than suggest, less personal than advise, and unlike prescribe it leaves the decision with the hearer.
entries.see also: suggest, advise, propose, prescribe, endorse

examples: The agent steered us toward properties well above our budget.
She steered the conversation away from politics.
He steered me away from taking the night shift.
A good editor steers a writer without rewriting them.
They steered the company through two recessions.
I'd steer clear of that intersection at rush hour.
Her advisor steered her toward applying a year early.
entries.русский: направлять, подводить к выбору — исподволь, не высказывая совета прямо
entries.type: reporting verb — guidance toward or away from
entries.patterns: steer + sb + toward/to + noun phrase or -ing · steer + sb + away from + noun phrase or -ing · steer + sb + through + noun phrase · steer clear of + noun phrase or -ing
entries.never: steer someone to do something and steer someone that. It is a preposition verb throughout; the infinitive frame does not exist, and neither does a clause of any kind — steer cannot carry what was actually said, only the direction it pushed.
entries.reports: guiding someone's choice without ever stating the advice outright — the word implies indirection, which is why it is the natural verb for a salesperson or a diplomat. Steer clear of is a fixed idiom meaning avoid entirely.
entries.see also: nudge, discourage, encourage, talk out of

examples: She suggested that we split the check.
He suggested meeting at the office instead.
The report suggests a link between the two events.
Can I suggest something?
Nobody suggested that the delay was deliberate.
I'd suggest leaving early if you want a seat.
She suggested to the committee that the vote be postponed.
He suggested where we might look next.
entries.pronunciation note: the /ɡ/ is pronounced in American English; British English usually drops it, /səˈdʒɛst/
entries.русский: предлагать; наводить на мысль — совет без нажима; о фактах — «свидетельствовать о»
entries.patterns: suggest + that-clause (subjunctive) · suggest + -ing · suggest + wh-clause · suggest + noun phrase · suggest + noun phrase + to + sb · suggest to + sb + that-clause
entries.never: suggest someone to do something — this is the single most common structural error in reported speech. Suggest takes no personal object at all before its complement: not with a bare object (✗ suggested me to leave), not with a preposition (✗ suggested to me to leave), not with a bare infinitive (✗ suggested me leave). Repairs: suggested that I leave, suggested leaving, suggested it to me. A second error rides alongside it: ✗ suggested us a restaurant → ✓ suggested a restaurant to us.
entries.subjunctive: American English takes the bare mandative form — suggested that he be there by nine, not that he should be, which is the British preference and reads as either stiff or oddly permissive to an American ear. The indicative means something entirely different: suggested that he was there by nine is a report of evidence, not a suggestion. That second sense is real and common — The data suggest that the drug works — and it is the only context in which the indicative after suggest is correct.
entries.reports: a proposal or recommendation offered without the authority implied by tell or the urgency of urge. In the evidential sense it reports what facts imply rather than what a person said.
entries.see also: recommend, propose, advise, float, put forward, insist, demand

examples: She talked me into buying the extended warranty.
He talked himself into believing the flight would be on time.
Don't let them talk you into anything you'll regret.
Somehow they talked the landlord into letting them paint.
I got talked into running the meeting.
Nobody talked her into it; it was her idea from the start.
entries.pronunciation note: in running speech into reduces to /ˈɪntə/, IN-tuh
entries.русский: уговорить (на что-л.) — разг.: уговоры подействовали, часто с оттенком сожаления
entries.patterns: talk + sb + into + -ing · talk + sb + into + noun phrase · talk + oneself + into + -ing
entries.never: talk someone into to do something and talk someone to do something. After into comes a gerund or a noun, never an infinitive. The object goes between talk and into: ✗ talked into it me.
entries.reports: persuasion that worked, in the register of ordinary speech, and usually with a shade of regret or amusement — he talked me into it rarely introduces a decision the speaker is proud of. The formal equivalents are persuade and prevail on.
entries.see also: talk out of, persuade, convince, prevail on, egg on

examples: His brother talked him out of selling the truck.
I talked myself out of calling her back.
She talked the crew out of walking off the job.
They tried to talk us out of the corner unit, which made us want it more.
He got talked out of it by someone who had done the drive before.
Nobody could talk her out of going.
entries.русский: отговорить (от чего-л.) — разг.: человек отказался от задуманного
entries.patterns: talk + sb + out of + -ing · talk + sb + out of + noun phrase · talk + oneself + out of + -ing
entries.never: talk someone out of to do something, talk someone from doing something, and talk someone out to do. The full preposition is out of, followed by a gerund or noun.
entries.reports: the everyday counterpart of dissuade — an argument that stopped somebody from doing what they had planned. Like dissuade, it is a success verb: the plan was abandoned.
entries.see also: talk into, dissuade, discourage, deter

examples: An employee tipped off investigators about the missing inventory.
She tipped me off that the position was about to be posted.
Somebody must have tipped them off.
He was tipped off to the raid an hour beforehand.
A neighbor tipped off the reporter, and the story ran that week.
The accent tipped me off that she wasn't from around there.
entries.pronunciation note: the noun is a tip-off, /ˈtɪp ɔf/, TIP-awf, with the stress moved forward and a hyphen
entries.русский: предупредить по секрету, «слить» информацию — разг., с оттенком осведомительства
entries.patterns: tip + sb + off · tip + sb + off + that-clause · tip + sb + off + about/to + noun phrase · tip off + noun phrase (unsplit, with a full noun object: tipped off investigators)
entries.never: tip off him — a pronoun object must sit inside the phrasal verb: tipped him off, never ✗ tipped off him. (A full noun phrase may go either side: tipped off investigators / tipped investigators off.) And tip off someone to do something: there is no infinitive frame, and no subjunctive — the that-clause states a fact.
entries.reports: passing on information privately, usually about something the hearer was not supposed to know or something illicit. The word carries a whiff of the informant — police are tipped off, reporters are tipped off — and it presupposes the information turned out to be worth having.
entries.see also: alert, warn, flag, forewarn, inform

examples: Officials urged residents along the coast to evacuate.
She urged me not to sign anything before Monday.
The letter urges that the hearing be rescheduled.
Her doctor urged caution about the dosage.
He kept urging the horse on.
I'd urge you to read the whole thing before deciding.
entries.русский: настоятельно призывать, убеждать — сильная рекомендация, без гарантии результата
entries.patterns: urge + sb + to-infinitive · urge + that-clause (subjunctive) · urge + noun phrase (urge caution) · urge + sb + on · urge + noun phrase + on/upon + sb (formal)
entries.never: urge someone doing something and urge someone from doing something. The negative is not to: urged us not to wait.
entries.subjunctive: urge is a full mandative trigger — urged that the report be released, urged that she not resign. British writing often has urged that he should be released; American writing does not.
entries.reports: recommending with pressure and often with urgency, and saying nothing about whether it worked. Urge is the standard verb of press releases and official statements (officials urged residents to evacuate), which is why it reads as slightly formal in conversation.
entries.see also: press, exhort, advise, encourage, warn, insist, demand

examples: The ranger warned us about the ice on the upper trail.
Forecasters warned that the storm could stall over the valley.
He warned her that the offer would expire at midnight.
Signs warn swimmers against going out past the buoys.
The guidebook warns against hiking the ridge after noon.
She warned me off the seafood, and she was right.
I warned him, and he did it anyway.
entries.русский: предупреждать — указать на опасность или дурные последствия, которых ещё можно избежать
entries.patterns: warn + sb + to-infinitive · warn + sb + not to-infinitive · warn + sb + that-clause · warn + that-clause · warn + sb + of/about + noun phrase or -ing · warn + (sb) + against + -ing · warn + sb + off
entries.never: warn someone from doing something — it is against: ✗ warned us from swimming there → ✓ warned us against swimming there. And warn someone to not do something; the negative goes before to. There is no subjunctive: ✗ warned that he be careful → ✓ warned him to be careful. Note that warn is the one warning verb in this file that takes both an infinitive and a clause, so both repairs are always open to it.
entries.reports: notice of a danger or a bad consequence, with the implication that the hearer can still avoid it. Stronger and more alarmed than caution, more consequential than alert — you alert someone to a fact, you warn them what the fact will cost. Note the objectless warn that, standard in news writing: Forecasters warned that the storm could stall.
entries.see also: caution, alert, forewarn, admonish, tip off, threaten

examples: Her presentation won over the two holdouts on the board.
It took a year to win the neighborhood over.
He won me over with the second draft.
The candidate is trying to win over voters who backed her opponent.
Nobody was won over by the apology.
She won them over to the idea of a shorter season.
entries.русский: переманить на свою сторону, расположить к себе — из противника сделать сторонника
entries.type: reporting verb — successful persuasion of an opponent
entries.patterns: win + sb + over · win over + noun phrase · win + sb + over to + noun phrase
entries.never: win someone over to do something and win someone over that. No infinitive, no clause — this verb reports a result and cannot carry the content of what was said. With a pronoun the particle follows: won her over, never won over her.
entries.reports: turning a skeptic or an opponent into a supporter. It says nothing about method and everything about the starting point — you can only win over somebody who was against you, which distinguishes it from persuade, where the hearer may simply have been undecided.
entries.see also: persuade, convince, prevail on, talk into
